source.title: Give and Take Feedback Well
source.attribution: A Reborn guide drawing on the Center for Creative Leadership, the US Office of Personnel Management, the UNC Chapel Hill Writing Center and the CDC.
source.notes: Written by Reborn in our own words; no text copied. References: Center for Creative Leadership, Use SBI (Situation-Behavior-Impact) to Inquire About Intent, https://www.ccl.org/articles/leading-effectively-articles/closing-the-gap-between-intent-vs-impact-sbii/; US Office of Personnel Management, Performance Management Cycle, https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/performance-management/performance-management-cycle/monitoring/; The Writing Center, UNC Chapel Hill, Getting Feedback, https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/getting-feedback/; CDC, Positive Parenting Tips, https://www.cdc.gov/child-development/positive-parenting-tips/index.html

cards.title: Good feedback helps people see what they can't see themselves
cards.body:
We all have blind spots. You can't hear how you sound in a meeting, see how your text landed or notice the habit that drives your flatmate mad. Feedback is how other people show you those things, and how you return the favour.

Done badly, feedback stings and gets ignored. Done well, it is one of the kindest things you can offer: a colleague learns why the client went quiet, a partner learns what makes you feel cared for, a child learns what 'tidy' actually means.

This guide covers how to give feedback that is specific, fair and timely, how to praise so it counts, how to adjust for managers, partners, children and friends, and how to take feedback, ask for it and act on it.
cards.apply_it: Think of one piece of feedback that genuinely helped you. Note what made it useful: who said it, how and when.

quiz.question: Why is feedback valuable?
options: It proves who is right in a disagreement
It shows people things they can't easily see in themselves
It replaces the need to talk in person
It is mainly a way to let off steam
quiz.explanation: Feedback works as a mirror. Others can see effects and habits that are hard to notice from the inside.

cards.title: Treat feedback as useful information, not a judgement on someone's worth
cards.body:
Many people hear 'feedback' and brace for a telling-off. That fear makes givers vague and receivers defensive. It helps to see feedback simply as information about how something worked, or didn't.

Compare 'You're hopeless with money' with 'We went over the food budget by forty pounds this month.' The first is a verdict on a person. The second is a fact you can both look at and do something about.

When you give feedback, aim to hand over information the other person can use. When you receive it, try to look for the information inside the message, even if it arrives wrapped in clumsy words. Both habits take the heat out of the conversation.
cards.apply_it: Next time you're about to criticise someone, ask yourself: 'What is the actual information I want them to have?'

quiz.question: Which statement is information rather than a verdict?
options: 'You're so disorganised'
'You always let people down'
'The report arrived two days after the deadline'
quiz.explanation: It describes what happened without judging the person, so it can be discussed and fixed.

cards.title: Describe what someone did, not what kind of person they are
cards.body:
Labels like 'lazy', 'rude' or 'selfish' feel accurate in the moment, but they attack character. People can't change who they are by Tuesday, so they defend themselves instead of listening.

Behaviour is different. 'You checked your phone three times while I was talking about my day' is something your partner can picture and choose to do differently. At work, 'You interrupted Priya twice in the meeting' is far more useful than 'You're arrogant.'

A quick test: could a camera have recorded it? If yes, you're describing behaviour. If it is an opinion about their personality or motives, rewrite it until it describes actions or words.
cards.apply_it: Take one complaint you have about someone and rewrite it so a camera could have recorded it.

quiz.question: What is the 'camera test' for feedback?
options: Checking whether your words describe something that could be observed
Recording the conversation for later
Giving feedback only on video calls
quiz.explanation: If a camera could have captured it, you are describing behaviour rather than labelling someone's character.

cards.title: Use situation, behaviour and impact to make feedback clear
cards.body:
A simple structure keeps feedback focused. Name the situation, describe the behaviour, then explain the impact it had. It is widely taught as the situation-behaviour-impact approach.

At work: 'In this morning's client call, when you shared the figures before I'd introduced them, the client looked confused and asked me to start again.' At home: 'Last night at dinner, when you corrected my story in front of your parents, I felt embarrassed and stopped talking.'

The situation anchors it to a real moment. The behaviour keeps it factual. The impact explains why it matters, which is the part people most often leave out. Without it, feedback can sound like nitpicking.
cards.apply_it: Draft one piece of feedback using the three parts: 'When... (situation), you... (behaviour), and the effect was... (impact).'

quiz.question: Which part of situation-behaviour-impact explains why the feedback matters?
options: The situation
The behaviour
The impact
The apology
quiz.explanation: The impact shows the effect of the behaviour, which gives the other person a reason to care about changing it.

cards.title: After describing the impact, ask what they meant to happen
cards.body:
You know the effect someone's actions had on you. You don't know what they were trying to do. A colleague who rewrote your slides may have thought they were helping. A friend who left the party early may have been feeling unwell.

So after describing what happened and its effect, add a genuine question: 'What were you aiming for there?' or 'How did it look from your side?' Then listen.

This turns feedback into a conversation rather than a charge sheet. Sometimes you'll learn something that changes your view entirely. Even when you don't, the other person feels treated fairly, which makes them far more likely to take the point on board.
cards.apply_it: In your next feedback conversation, end with one honest question such as 'How did it look from your side?'

quiz.question: Why ask about the other person's intention after giving feedback?
options: To trap them into admitting fault
Because you can see the impact but not what they were trying to do
So you can skip describing the behaviour
quiz.explanation: Asking about intent fills the gap in what you know and keeps the conversation fair and two-way.

cards.title: Give feedback soon, while the moment is still fresh
cards.body:
Feedback loses value with age. If you mention in March that a colleague's January presentation ran long, they will barely remember it, and may wonder why you've been holding on to it.

Aim for the same day or the next, when the details are clear for both of you. 'Can I mention something from the meeting just now?' works better than saving a list for a yearly review.

The exception is when emotions are high. If you're furious with your partner about the forgotten school pick-up, wait until you can speak calmly, perhaps after the children are in bed. Timely means soon enough to be useful, not so soon that you say things you regret.
cards.apply_it: If you've been holding back a piece of feedback for weeks, either share it this week or decide to let it go.

quiz.question: When is the best time to give feedback?
options: Soon after the event, once you're calm
Months later, at a formal review
Only when you have a long list
Immediately, even if you're very angry
quiz.explanation: Feedback is most useful when the moment is fresh, but it should wait until you can speak calmly.

cards.title: Give critical feedback in private, not in front of others
cards.body:
Being corrected in front of people adds embarrassment to the message, and embarrassment makes people defend themselves rather than listen. Your point gets lost in their need to save face.

So pick a private moment. Pull a teammate aside after the meeting rather than challenging them in front of the group. Raise the comment about your friend's jokes when it's just the two of you, not at the pub table. With a child, a quiet word away from siblings usually works better than a public telling-off.

Private doesn't mean secret or formal. A short walk, a quick call or a quiet corner is enough. The aim is to let the person hear you without an audience.
cards.apply_it: Next time you need to correct someone, wait for a moment when it's just the two of you.

quiz.question: Why is critical feedback usually better in private?
options: It is easier to exaggerate when no one else is listening
It means you never have to follow up
An audience adds embarrassment, which makes people defensive
quiz.explanation: Without an audience, people can focus on the message instead of protecting their reputation.

cards.title: Focus on one thing at a time
cards.body:
When we finally pluck up courage to give feedback, it's tempting to unload everything: the late reports, the messy desk and that comment from last summer. The other person hears an attack and remembers none of it.

Pick the one point that matters most and leave the rest for another day. If your teenager's room is chaotic, start with the dirty plates rather than listing every problem. If a new colleague's emails are confusing, focus on subject lines first.

One clear point is easy to take in and act on. Once it improves, you have a success to build on, and the next conversation feels easier for both of you.
cards.apply_it: Before your next feedback chat, write down all your points, then circle just one to raise.

quiz.question: Why focus on one point when giving feedback?
options: One clear point is easier to take in and act on
It means you never mention the other issues
People only have room for criticism once a year
quiz.explanation: A single focused point is easier to remember and change, and early success makes later conversations easier.

cards.title: Point towards what to do next, not only what went wrong
cards.body:
Feedback that only looks backwards leaves people knowing they got it wrong but unsure what right looks like. Add a forward-looking part: what would work better next time?

'The report was hard to follow' becomes useful when you add 'Next time, could you put the recommendation on the first page?' Telling a child 'Don't be so loud' helps less than 'Use your indoor voice while the baby's asleep.'

You can also ask rather than tell: 'What might you try next time?' People often have good ideas, and they're more committed to a plan they came up with themselves. Either way, end with a clear, doable next step.
cards.apply_it: In your next piece of criticism, add one sentence that starts 'Next time, could you...'

quiz.question: What makes feedback more useful than just pointing out a mistake?
options: Repeating the mistake several times
Comparing them with someone better
Adding a clear idea of what to do next time
quiz.explanation: A forward-looking step shows what good looks like, so the person knows how to improve.

cards.title: Make praise specific so people know what to repeat
cards.body:
'Great job!' feels nice for a moment, but it tells the person nothing. Did you like the speed, the detail, the tone? They can't repeat what they can't identify.

Specific praise uses the same pattern as criticism: what they did and the effect it had. 'Your summary at the top of the email meant I could reply in two minutes.' 'You remembered to ask about my mum's operation, and it made me feel really looked after.'

Specific praise is also more believable. Vague compliments can sound automatic or even sarcastic. Details show you were paying attention, which is often what people value most.
cards.apply_it: Today, swap one 'Well done' for a sentence naming exactly what someone did and why it helped.

quiz.question: Why is specific praise better than 'Great job'?
options: It takes longer to say
It tells the person exactly what to keep doing
It avoids any emotional content
It works only at work
quiz.explanation: Naming the behaviour and its effect shows the person what to repeat and proves you noticed.

cards.title: Praise choices and effort more than talent
cards.body:
There's a difference between 'You're so clever' and 'You kept trying different ways until the puzzle worked.' The first is about a fixed quality. The second is about something the person did and can do again.

Many educators and parenting experts suggest focusing praise on effort, strategy and choices, especially with children. A child praised for persistence learns that sticking at things pays off. One praised only for being clever may avoid hard tasks in case they fail.

The same applies to adults. 'You stayed calm when that customer shouted' gives a colleague something to build on. 'You're a natural' is pleasant, but it offers no guidance.
cards.apply_it: Next time you praise a child or colleague, name something they chose to do rather than a talent they have.

quiz.question: Which is an example of praising effort or choices?
options: 'You're a born genius'
'You're just naturally good at this'
'You practised every evening and it shows'
quiz.explanation: It points to a choice the person made, which they can repeat in future.

cards.title: Avoid hiding criticism inside a compliment sandwich
cards.body:
The compliment sandwich puts criticism between two bits of praise: 'Great presentation! The figures were wrong. But lovely slides!' It feels gentler to say, but it often backfires.

People tend to remember either the praise or the criticism, not both. Some miss the real point entirely. Others learn that your praise is just padding, so they stop trusting it. A friend who always hears 'I love it, but...' starts waiting for the 'but'.

Instead, keep them separate and honest. Give praise when it's earned, on its own. Give criticism clearly and kindly, on its own. Warmth comes from your tone and respect, not from wrapping.
cards.apply_it: Notice if you're about to start criticism with 'I love it, but...'. Give the praise and the point separately instead.

quiz.question: What is a common problem with the compliment sandwich?
options: People may miss the criticism or stop trusting the praise
It makes feedback far too short
It only works in writing
It is too direct
quiz.explanation: Mixing praise and criticism can blur the message and make future praise sound like padding.

cards.title: Check the other person is ready to hear it
cards.body:
Feedback dropped on someone who is rushing, stressed or upset rarely lands. Your colleague racing to a deadline or your friend who has just had bad news can't take it in.

A simple check helps: 'Have you got five minutes? I'd like to mention something about the handover.' Or with a partner: 'Is now a good time to talk about the weekend plans?' If they say no, agree a time.

Asking gives people a moment to prepare and a sense of control. It also signals respect. A message they've agreed to hear is much easier to take than one that ambushes them halfway up the stairs.
cards.apply_it: Before your next feedback conversation, ask 'Is now a good time?' and accept the answer.

quiz.question: Why ask 'Is now a good time?' before giving feedback?
options: It lets them avoid the conversation forever
It makes the feedback sound less important
It gives them a chance to be ready, which helps them listen
quiz.explanation: People who have agreed to the conversation are calmer and more able to take in what you say.

cards.title: Say your piece briefly, then stop and let them respond
cards.body:
Nervous feedback givers often keep talking: explaining, softening, repeating and justifying. The longer you go on, the more it feels like a lecture.

Make your point in a few sentences, then stop. 'In yesterday's stand-up, you said the bug was fixed before it was tested, and the client found it this morning. What happened?' Then pause and let the silence do some work.

This matters at home too. Telling a flatmate about the washing-up needs about thirty seconds, not a ten-minute speech. Short feedback feels respectful and leaves room for their side, which is where the useful conversation usually begins.
cards.apply_it: Time your next piece of feedback. Aim to say the main point in under thirty seconds, then pause.

quiz.question: What should you do after stating your feedback?
options: Keep explaining until they agree
Stop and give them space to respond
Leave immediately
Repeat it in different words
quiz.explanation: Stopping turns a lecture into a conversation and invites their side of the story.

cards.title: Be careful giving critical feedback in writing
cards.body:
Written criticism loses your tone of voice and your face. 'The draft needs work' might be friendly in person but can read as cold in an email or chat message. The reader often fills the gap with the worst interpretation.

For anything sensitive, talk first, by phone, video or in person, then follow up in writing if a record helps. 'Thanks for the chat. As agreed, you'll send the revised plan by Friday.'

Written feedback works well for detailed, practical comments, like edits on a document. Even then, add a line of context and warmth: 'Mostly small tweaks, the structure works well.' And never send critical feedback when you're annoyed.
cards.apply_it: Before sending any critical message, ask: would this be better as a quick call?

quiz.question: What is a good approach to sensitive feedback?
options: Send a long email so it's all on record
Text it late at night when you think of it
Talk first, then follow up in writing if needed
quiz.explanation: Speaking lets tone and warmth come through, and a written follow-up can confirm what was agreed.

cards.title: Give feedback to your manager by focusing on shared goals
cards.body:
Telling your boss something isn't working can feel risky, but most good managers want to know. The trick is to link your point to something they care about.

Instead of 'Your last-minute requests are unfair', try 'When tasks arrive on Friday afternoon, I can't do them well and quality drops. Could we flag them by Thursday?' It's about the work, not their character, and it offers a solution.

Pick a calm moment, perhaps a regular one-to-one, and ask first: 'Can I share something that would help me do better work?' Keep it to one point, and be willing to hear their view. Upward feedback done this way often earns respect.
cards.apply_it: In your next one-to-one, ask your manager if you can share one thing that would help you work better.

quiz.question: How can you make feedback to a manager more likely to land?
options: Link it to shared goals and suggest a solution
Raise it in a big meeting so others back you up
Wait until you're leaving the job
quiz.explanation: Connecting the point to goals you share and offering a fix makes it constructive rather than a complaint.

cards.title: Give feedback to a partner as a request, not a criticism
cards.body:
With partners, feedback can quickly slide into old arguments. 'You never listen' sparks a defence of every time they did listen.

It helps to frame it as a specific request about the future: 'When I'm telling you about work and you look at your phone, I feel like it doesn't matter. Could we put phones away at dinner?' That names the behaviour, its effect and what you'd like instead.

Avoid words like 'always' and 'never', and choose a calm moment rather than mid-row. And remember to give positive feedback too. 'I loved that you booked the restaurant without me asking' builds the goodwill that makes harder conversations easier.
cards.apply_it: Turn one complaint about your partner into a specific request that starts 'Could we...'

quiz.question: Which is the most helpful way to give feedback to a partner?
options: 'You never listen to me'
'Everyone says you're a bad listener'
'When you look at your phone while I talk, I feel ignored. Could we put phones away at dinner?'
quiz.explanation: It names a specific behaviour, its effect and a clear request, without 'never' or outside judgement.

cards.title: Give children clear, simple feedback about what to do
cards.body:
Children often hear feedback as a verdict on whether they're good or bad. Keep it about the action and short enough to remember.

Instead of 'You're so naughty', try 'Throwing toys can hurt someone. Put them in the box, please.' Rather than 'Your room's a disgrace', say 'Clothes go in the basket and books on the shelf.' Clear instructions show what success looks like.

Catch them getting it right as often as you correct them. 'You shared your crayons with your sister without being asked, that was kind' teaches more than a dozen reminders. Public health guidance for parents often highlights praising good behaviour as one of the most useful tools you have.
cards.apply_it: Today, notice your child doing something right and describe it out loud to them.

quiz.question: What is a good way to correct a young child?
options: Tell them they're naughty
Describe the action and say what to do instead
Ignore it and hope it stops
List everything else they've done wrong
quiz.explanation: Short, specific feedback about the action and a clear alternative helps children know what to do.

cards.title: Give feedback to friends gently and only when it helps them
cards.body:
Friends haven't signed up to be managed, so think before giving unrequested feedback. Ask yourself: is this something they'd want to know, and is it about something they can change?

A friend with spinach in their teeth before a date wants to know. A friend's choice of partner or haircut may not be your business unless they ask. When it does matter, perhaps a habit of cancelling plans at the last minute, raise it privately and warmly: 'I really value our evenings, and it's hard when plans change on the day. Is everything OK?'

Lead with care, keep it to one point and leave room for them to explain.
cards.apply_it: Before offering a friend feedback, ask yourself: would they want to know, and can they act on it?

quiz.question: When is unrequested feedback to a friend most appropriate?
options: When it's about something they'd want to know and can change
Whenever you disagree with their choices
Only in a group so others can weigh in
quiz.explanation: Friends value feedback that is useful and actionable, offered with care, not opinions on every choice.

cards.title: Give peers feedback as an equal, not as their boss
cards.body:
Feedback between colleagues at the same level can feel awkward. You don't want to sound like you're managing them, yet staying silent lets problems grow.

Speak as a teammate who shares the goal. 'I noticed the shared folder hasn't been updated since Monday, and I wasted an hour on an old version. Could we agree to update it daily?' This is about the work, and you've included yourself in the fix.

Peer praise matters just as much. 'Your notes from the workshop saved me redoing my slides, thank you' builds trust across the team. The more normal everyday feedback becomes, the less awkward the harder conversations feel.
cards.apply_it: Give one colleague a specific thank-you today for something that made your work easier.

quiz.question: How should you give feedback to a colleague at the same level?
options: As a teammate focused on the shared goal
As if you were their manager
Only through your boss
quiz.explanation: Framing it as a shared problem keeps it equal and practical, without overstepping.

cards.title: Notice the urge to defend yourself when feedback arrives
cards.body:
When someone criticises us, the body often reacts before the mind does. Your face gets hot, your chest tightens and a list of excuses lines up: 'But I was busy', 'You do it too.'

This reaction is normal, but acting on it closes the conversation. Your manager stops giving you useful pointers. Your partner decides it's not worth raising things.

The first step is just to notice the urge. Take a breath. Remind yourself that you can listen fully now and decide later whether you agree. Listening isn't the same as accepting every word. It just means you hear the whole message before responding.
cards.apply_it: Next time you receive criticism, take one slow breath before saying anything.

quiz.question: What is the first step to receiving feedback well?
options: Explaining why the other person is wrong
Agreeing with everything immediately
Noticing the urge to defend yourself and pausing
Changing the subject
quiz.explanation: Pausing gives you a chance to listen instead of reacting, without committing you to agree.

cards.title: Say thank you and ask for an example
cards.body:
A simple response helps when feedback is hard to hear: 'Thanks for telling me. Can you give me an example?' It buys you time and gets you more useful detail.

Vague feedback like 'You come across as negative in meetings' is hard to act on. Asking 'Can you think of a moment when that happened?' might reveal that it's about how you respond to new ideas, which is something you can work on.

At home, if your partner says you're 'never around', ask what they mean. It might be the evenings on your laptop, not the hours you work. Thanking people also makes them more likely to give you feedback again.
cards.apply_it: Practise saying 'Thanks for telling me. Can you give me an example?' so it's ready when you need it.

quiz.question: Why ask for an example when receiving vague feedback?
options: To get specific detail you can act on
To catch the other person out
To delay the conversation forever
quiz.explanation: An example turns a general impression into something concrete you can understand and change.

cards.title: Look for the useful part even when feedback is clumsy
cards.body:
Not everyone gives feedback well. It may arrive as a sarcastic remark, a sweeping 'always' or a comment made at the worst moment. It's tempting to dismiss the whole thing because of how it was said.

Try to separate the message from the delivery. Your brother's 'You're obsessed with your phone' is unkind, but is there something in it? A customer's angry email may still point to a real gap in your service.

Ask yourself: if a calm, kind person had said this, would part of it be fair? You can still tell the other person how their delivery felt. But don't throw away useful information because it came in poor packaging.
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent clumsy criticism. Write down one part of it that might be fair.

quiz.question: What should you do with feedback that is badly delivered?
options: Ignore it completely
Respond in the same tone
Separate the delivery from the message and look for anything fair
quiz.explanation: Poor delivery doesn't make the content wrong. Looking past it can reveal something useful.

cards.title: You don't have to agree with feedback on the spot
cards.body:
Some feedback is spot on. Some is partly right. Some says more about the giver than about you. You don't need to decide which in the moment.

It's fine to say: 'That's useful, I want to think it over.' Then reflect later. Does it match what others have said? Is there a pattern? A single comment from a tired friend might be a one-off. The same point from your manager, partner and best friend probably deserves attention.

If, after thought, you disagree, you can go back and explain calmly: 'I thought about what you said. I see it differently, and here's why.' Taking it seriously doesn't mean accepting all of it.
cards.apply_it: When you next get feedback you're unsure about, say 'Let me think that over' and revisit it within two days.

quiz.question: How can you judge whether a piece of feedback is accurate?
options: Check whether others have noticed the same pattern
Decide instantly based on how you feel
Accept everything without question
Reject anything that feels uncomfortable
quiz.explanation: A pattern across several people is a strong sign the feedback deserves attention.

cards.title: Accept praise with a simple thank you
cards.body:
Many of us brush off compliments: 'Oh, it was nothing', 'I just got lucky', 'Anyone could have done it.' It might feel modest, but it can leave the other person feeling dismissed, as if their judgement was wrong.

Try a plain 'Thank you, I'm really glad it helped.' If a colleague praises your report, you can add something like 'Thanks, I worked hard on the summary.' If a friend loves the meal you made, simply enjoy it.

Accepting praise also helps you learn. Positive feedback tells you what's working, so it deserves as much attention as criticism. Notice what people thank you for and do more of it.
cards.apply_it: The next time someone compliments you, say 'Thank you' and stop there.

quiz.question: Why is it worth accepting praise rather than brushing it off?
options: Dismissing it can leave the giver feeling ignored, and praise shows you what works
It makes you look arrogant
Praise is never accurate
quiz.explanation: Accepting praise respects the giver and helps you notice your strengths.

cards.title: Ask for feedback with a specific question
cards.body:
'Any feedback?' usually gets 'No, all good.' People don't want to offend you and don't know where to start.

A narrower question makes it easier: 'What's one thing I could do to make my updates more useful?' or 'Was there a point in my talk where you lost interest?' At home: 'Is there one thing I could do that would make mornings less stressful for you?'

Asking for 'one thing' makes the request feel small and safe. Asking about something specific shows you're genuinely open. And asking soon after an event, while it's fresh, gets better answers than waiting for a yearly review.
cards.apply_it: Ask one person today: 'What's one thing I could do better at...?' and name a specific task.

quiz.question: Which request is most likely to get useful feedback?
options: 'Any feedback?'
'Was everything fine?'
'Is there anything else?'
'What's one thing that would make my reports easier to use?'
quiz.explanation: A specific, small request is easier to answer honestly and gives you something concrete to work on.

cards.title: Ask a range of people, and ask regularly
cards.body:
If you only ask people who like everything you do, you'll only hear good news. If you only ask once a year, you'll miss the small adjustments that make the biggest difference.

Try asking different people for different views. A colleague can tell you how you come across in meetings, a customer how clear your instructions are, a friend how good you are at keeping in touch. Each sees a different side of you.

Make it a habit rather than an event. A quick 'How did that go from your side?' after a meeting, a family dinner or a shared project keeps the feedback small, frequent and easy to act on.
cards.apply_it: Pick one person you don't usually ask for feedback and ask them a short, specific question this week.

quiz.question: Why ask several different people for feedback?
options: Each sees a different side of you, so you get a fuller picture
So you can choose the most flattering answer
Because one person's view is always wrong
quiz.explanation: Different people notice different things, which helps you spot patterns and blind spots.

cards.title: Make it safe for people to tell you the truth
cards.body:
People decide whether to give you honest feedback based on what happened last time. If you argued, sulked or went quiet, they'll think twice before trying again.

Your reaction is the signal. Thank them, even if it stung. Ask questions rather than defending. Later, show that you did something with it. A team leader who says 'Thanks, you were right about the deadline, I've moved it' will hear far more than one who bristles.

The same applies with family. If your teenager tells you that your questions feel like interrogations, and you respond calmly, they're more likely to open up next time. Safety is built one reaction at a time.
cards.apply_it: After the next feedback you receive, thank the person and tell them one thing you'll do about it.

quiz.question: What most affects whether people keep giving you honest feedback?
options: How long you've known them
Whether you ask in writing
How senior you are
How you reacted the last time they did
quiz.explanation: People judge whether it's safe to be honest based on how you responded before.

cards.title: Turn feedback into one small, concrete change
cards.body:
Feedback is only useful if something changes. But 'be more confident' or 'listen better' is too vague to act on.

Translate it into a specific behaviour you can try this week. 'You talk over people in meetings' could become 'I'll wait until someone finishes and count to two before speaking.' 'You're always on your phone' might become 'Phone goes in the drawer from six until the kids are in bed.'

Pick one change, not five. Write it down somewhere you'll see it. Small, clear changes are easier to stick to, and they show others you've taken their feedback seriously.
cards.apply_it: Take one piece of recent feedback and write down a single behaviour you'll change this week.

quiz.question: How should you act on feedback like 'You don't listen enough'?
options: Promise to be a completely different person
Wait to see if they mention it again
Turn it into one small, specific behaviour to try
quiz.explanation: A concrete action is easier to do and to notice than a vague intention.

cards.title: Follow up so feedback becomes a conversation, not a one-off
cards.body:
After giving or receiving feedback, come back to it. Without a follow-up, both people are left wondering whether it mattered.

If you received feedback, return after a week or two: 'You mentioned my updates were too long. I've been putting the key point first. Is that better?' This shows you listened and gives them a chance to say more.

If you gave it, notice improvement and say so: 'I saw you let Priya finish her points today, that really helped the discussion.' At home: 'Thanks for putting your phone away at dinner, I've loved our chats.' Following up turns a hard moment into progress you both share.
cards.apply_it: Think of feedback you gave or received recently and check in with the person about it this week.

quiz.question: Why is following up on feedback important?
options: It shows the feedback mattered and lets you both see progress
It lets you repeat the criticism
It is only needed for formal reviews
quiz.explanation: Following up closes the loop, recognises change and keeps the conversation going.

cards.title: Practise feedback daily in small doses
cards.body:
Feedback gets easier with practice, and small daily habits beat rare big conversations. Try this simple routine.

Each day, give one piece of specific praise: name what someone did and the difference it made. It might be a colleague's clear message, a child's patience or a partner's thoughtful gesture.

Then, once a week, ask one person one specific question about how you're doing, listen without defending and say thank you. When something needs correcting, use situation, behaviour and impact, say it soon and in private, and follow up.

Over time, honest feedback stops feeling like a big event. It becomes part of how you care for people, at work and at home.
cards.apply_it: Start today: give one specific piece of praise and note who you'll ask for feedback this week.

quiz.question: What is a simple daily feedback habit?
options: Saving all comments for an annual review
Giving one piece of specific praise each day
Criticising one person every day
Avoiding feedback until a problem is serious
quiz.explanation: Daily specific praise builds the skill and goodwill that make harder feedback easier.
